'''Rodney Dewayne Priestley''' (born 1979) is an American chemical engineer and professor at [[Princeton University]]. His research considers the phase transitions of polymers and their application in electronic devices and healthcare. In 2020 he was made the [[Princeton University]] Vice Dean of Innovation. He was named dean of [[Princeton University Graduate School| The Graduate School]] effective June 1, 2022.

== Early life and education ==
Priestley grew up watching documentaries on [[National Geographic (American TV channel)|National Geographic]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Emerging Scholars {{!}} Diverse|url=https://diverseeducation.com/?emerging-scholar=dr-rodney-priestley-exemplifies-the-rigor-of-research-in-the-ivy-leagues|access-date=2020-07-23|website=diverseeducation.com}}</ref> He originally considered studying [[marine biology]] or [[geology]].<ref name=":0" /> During high school he became increasingly interested in chemistry.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=September 2014|url=http://www.asee-prism.org/2014/09/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=www.asee-prism.org}}</ref> Priestley eventually studied chemical engineering at [[Texas Tech University]] and graduated in 2003, where he competed in [[long jump]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Alumni News|url=https://www.depts.ttu.edu/che/department/news/alumni_news.php|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=|website=Texas Tech}}</ref> As part of a [[Research Experiences for Undergraduates]] programme at the [[University of Connecticut]] Priestley first encountered polymers, in the context of a project to develop artificial bone materials.<ref name=":0" /> He completed his doctoral degree at [[Northwestern University]], where he studied nanoscale confinement of polymers. In particular, Priestley made use of [[Fluorescence spectroscopy|fluorescence]] and [[dielectric spectroscopy]] to investigate how confinement and interfacial effects impacted the [[glass transition]] temperature and physical ageing of polymers.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=Effects of nanoscale confinement and interfaces on the structural relaxation of amorphous polymers monitored at the molecular scale by fluorescence and dielectric spectroscopy.|date=2008|language=English|first=Rodney Dewayne|last=Priestley|oclc=466441508}}</ref> Priestley was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Ecole Superieure de Physique et de Chimie Industrielles de la Ville de Paris]] (ESPCI).<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-08-04|title=Rodney Priestley|url=https://www.aiche.org/community/bio/rodney-priestley|access-date=2020-07-23|website=www.aiche.org|language=en}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
In 2009 Priestley returned to the [[United States]] and joined the faculty at [[Princeton University]]. At Princeton, Priestley studies the nanoscale properties of materials, and how to tune these for novel device applications.<ref name=":1" /> He has continued to study the [[glass transition]] temperatures of polymers, with a focus on the controlled formation of thin films and nanocolloids.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/units/dpoly/awards/recipient.cfm|access-date=2020-07-23|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref> Priestley has studied the transition temperatures of substances that are composed of two or more polymers, attaching fluorescent reporting tags to the different components and using the brightness of the tag to infer whether the polymer is in a glassy or rubbery phase.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=Doctoral research helps develop tool to probe plastics' behavior down to the molecular scale|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2019/03/08/doctoral-research-helps-develop-tool-probe-plastics-behavior-down-molecular-scale|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Princeton University|language=en}}</ref> As part of this work, Priestley studied [[plexiglas]], a composite system of [[poly(methyl methacrylate)]] (PMMA) and [[poly(butyl methacrylate)]] (PBMA) that is found in [[coronary stent]]s and paints.<ref name=":2" /> He combines experimental studies with computational investigations to better understand the distribution of the PMMA and PBMA throughout the plexiglass.<ref name=":2" /> Through his understanding of phase transitions, Priestley has shown that it is possible to precisely control nanostructures, and realised self-assembled biopolymers for use in [[artificial skin]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Schmidt fund awarded to two transformative bioengineering projects|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2019/06/10/schmidt-fund-awarded-two-transformative-bioengineering-projects|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Princeton University|language=en}}</ref>  Alongside his work on polymeric systems, Priestley has investigated nanoparticles, specifically engineered nanoscale [[zerovalent iron]] (enZVI) particles, as a means to clean groundwater.<ref>{{Cite web|title=PEI awards $1.01 million in Water and the Environment Grand Challenge projects|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2019/10/02/pei-awards-101-million-water-and-environment-grand-challenge-projects|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Princeton University|language=en}}</ref> He proposed the use of [[Janus particles]] for the use in [[surfactant]]-free cleansing.<ref>{{Cite web|title=WIPO Publishes Patent of the Trustees of Princeton University for "Janus Particles and Their Use for Surfactant-Free Cleansing and Emulsion Stabilization" (American Investors)|url=https://www.researchwithnj.com/en/clippings/wipo-publishes-patent-of-the-trustees-of-princeton-university-for-5|access-date=2020-07-23|website=New Jersey Research Community|language=en}}</ref>

In 2019 Priestley was promoted to full professor, and was one of the first African-Americans to hold such a position at [[Princeton University]].<ref name=":0" /> In 2020 he was made vice dean of innovation, and in 2022 named dean of [[Princeton University Graduate School|The Graduate School]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-09-18|title=Rodney Priestly|url=https://diverseeducation.com/article/155191/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Diverse|language=en}}</ref><ref name="TGS Appointment">{{cite web |last1=Valenti |first1=Denise |title=Rodney Priestley named dean of Princeton's Graduate School |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2022/03/09/rodney-priestley-named-dean-princetons-graduate-school |website=Princeton University |access-date=March 9, 2022}}</ref> He is the founder of the science-based Cativa health [[cannabidiol]].<ref>{{Cite web|first=Sam|last=Webb|date=2019-08-27|title=Cativa launches 'science-based' CBD brand|url=https://theleafdesk.com/cativa-launches-science-based-cbd-brand/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=The Leaf Desk|language=en}}</ref> Priestley is an associate editor of ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society|JACS]] Au'', an open-access journal.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-02-02|title=Celebrating African American Chemists: Rodney D. Priestley|url=https://axial.acs.org/2021/02/02/celebrating-african-american-chemists-rodney-d-priestley/|access-date=2021-02-05|website=ACS Axial|language=en-US}}</ref>
